newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan minister says profile-raising to continue.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan minister says profile-raising to continue.

text.p: Taiwan Foreign Minister John Chang, returning from his second overseas trip in a week, brushed aside Chinese protests on Sunday and said his ministry would do its utmost to raise the island's international profile.
Chang had left Taiwan for Malaysia quietly on Friday, a day after he returned from a surprise visit to Jakarta where he met Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas.

"The foreign ministry will make every effort to enlarge the room for us to take part on the international stage," Chang told journalists after he arrived at Taipei's international airport, adding that he would continue to visit countries that do not recognise Taiwan, including ones in Europe, Africa and Asia.

Chang said he met "a lot of friends" in Kuala Lumpur but was tight-lipped about identities, saying his reticence was at Malaysia's request. Local media reported that Chang had met his Malaysian counterpart.

"The Chinese mainland should not react that strongly. We have to make it gradually accept and get used to the fact of Republic of China (Taiwan) officials travelling abroad," Chang said earlier in transit at Singapore airport.

China, which sees Taiwan as a Chinese province and not entitled to foreign ties, had made serious representations to Indonesia, although Alatas stressed that his meeting with Chang was in a private capacity and Jakarta recognises only Beijing.
"The trips (to Indonesia and Malaysia)...helped mutual understanding and will help future relations," Chang said in comments in Singapore broadcast on Taiwanese television.

Taiwan lost its last Asian diplomatic ally, South Korea, in 1992 when Seoul switched diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing, but keeps close economic ties with many Asian countries where Taiwanese business executives have poured millions of dollars of investment in recent years.

Despite huge regional investment, Taiwan has tried in vain to have its president attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum meetings held in Southeast Asian countries, due to pressure from China.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin said on Friday that Taipei should prove it was sincere in its desire for senior-level talks by ending efforts to raise its international profile and climb out of its isolation.
Chang is a grandson of the late Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek, who fled to Taiwan in 1949 after the defeat of his armies by the communists in the Chinese civil war.
Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a rebel province since then and has tried to isolate the island diplomatically. Only 30 countries recognise Taiwan's Republic of China government.
Chang's trip to Indonesia and Malaysia followed a secret visit to the former Soviet republic of Ukraine in late August by Taiwan Vice President Lien Chan, which angered China.
China protested to Jakarta after Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui made an unofficial visit to Indonesia in 1994.
Lee's private but high-profile visit to the United States in mid-1995 prompted China to conduct war games near Taiwan, warning the island not to drop a pledge for reunification with Beijing.
Semi-official talks between the rivals -- both say they want reunification but under different terms -- have been suspended by an angry Beijing since mid-1995.
